paras: The Halifax watermelon poisoning was the death of a Black man and the serious illness of five others in Halifax County, Virginia, in early August 1880, after they ate watermelons laced with strychnine from a white man's patch beside a Black religious gathering. The owner, named in a wire report as Mr. Brashe or Brash, had posted placards warning that the melons were poisoned after blaming the meeting's attendees for their disappearance. The story ran widely in the white press through August, mostly as a tale about melon stealing, and no report of an arrest or charge against the owner appears in the coverage.

According to the Danville (Va.) News, Black residents of Halifax County were holding an "association" of a religious nature, and many gathered daily close to a watermelon patch owned by a white man. A dispatch dated Halifax, Virginia, August 7 described the gatherings as three days of "bush meetings" in the woods near the patch of a Mr. Brashe. When his melons began to disappear, the owner connected their loss with the people at the meeting.

According to the dispatch, he said nothing but, two days before its date, set up several large placards in the patch reading "Look out; these watermelons are poisoned." The melons had been injected with strychnine through punctures too fine to be seen. Taking the signs for an attempt to scare them off, some of the meeting's attendees ate the melons anyway.

One man, named in the wire as John Cumberland, died, and Sampson Jones, Alliston Alexander, Jeremiah Washington, Lycurgus Milburn and James Josephs were reported in dangerous condition. The Chicago Tribune's summary of the case said outright that Brashe "poisoned the melons," whether "to test the accuracy of his suspicions or to punish the robbers."
No report of an inquest, arrest, charge or trial appears in the coverage, and no later word on the five sick men was found.

The story first appeared in Virginia, where the Alexandria Gazette summarized the Danville News account on August 6, and the Washington Evening Star printed the Danville text the next day under the headline "Horrible Tale from Virginia." A fuller telegraphic version naming the dead and the sick followed on August 8 and 9 in the Chicago Tribune, the St. Paul Daily Globe and the Wheeling Register. Over the next month the Danville text and paraphrases of it were reprinted in papers in Delaware, West Virginia, Pennsylvania, Connecticut and Arizona Territory.

Most headlines treated the deaths lightly or as a lesson about theft. The Wheeling Register headed its copy "Fatal Effect of the Seductive Watermelon on Some Colored Brethren at a Virginia 'Bush-Meeting,'" while the Daily Globe ran it under "Deviltries and Disasters" as a "startling episode" in which worshipers were "Poisoned by Stolen Watermelons." The Tribune's news digest called the victims "Watermelon Thieves," and the Weekly Arizona Citizen titled its reprint "A Deadly Remedy for Melon Stealing." None of these accounts questioned the owner's act or mentioned any legal consequence, and all of the coverage found came from white papers.

The Halifax datelines of the wire and the Danville News attribution place the poisoning in Virginia, while the Tribune's summary, copied by the Canton Register, placed it at "Halifax Court-House, N. C."; the dated dispatches and the nearby Danville paper are the stronger evidence. The number gravely ill was five named men in the wire but "four or five" in the Danville account. Because the Danville report of a death was in print in Alexandria on August 6, the wire's statement that Cumberland died "last night" under an August 7 dateline leaves the exact day uncertain.

reader.title: Halifax watermelon poisoning
bases: One white landowner is reported to have injected his melons with strychnine, killing one Black man and sickening five who ate them near a Black religious meeting; no mob, band or officers were involved (A2, A4, A5).

The Danville News account (A1, A2) and a separately worded Halifax-dated wire with names (A4, A6, A7) agree on the placards, the strychnine, one death and several gravely ill, though both may rest on the same local information.

accounts.label: Danville (Va.) News
accounts.gist: Black residents of Halifax County at a religious 'association' were blamed by a white man for his vanishing melons; after his poison placard, some ate anyway, one died and four or five were in danger from strychnine.

accounts.label: Wire dispatch from Halifax, Va.
accounts.gist: After three days of 'bush meetings' near Mr. Brashe's patch, he posted placards; the eaters laughed them off, John Cumberland died and five named men lay in dangerous condition.

accounts.label: Chicago Tribune summary
accounts.gist: Mr. Brashe of Halifax Court-House, N.C., poisoned the melons either to test his suspicions or to punish 'the robbers'; one died, five precarious.

framing.detail: The Danville News text ran as 'Horrible Tale from Virginia' in Washington and Wilmington, without comment on the owner.

The Wheeling Register headed the wire 'Fatal Effect of the Seductive Watermelon on Some Colored Brethren' and the St. Paul Globe filed it under 'Deviltries and Disasters', a jocular treatment of the deaths.
The Chicago Tribune called the victims 'Watermelon Thieves' and 'the robbers' while stating plainly that Brashe poisoned the melons.
Later reprints carried titles such as 'A Deadly Remedy for Melon Stealing' and 'Dangerous Melons'.
